title: L6 Quarter-Review: Organized Code
story: You've mastered interfaces, modules, visibility, and library design. Your code is now organized like a professional project — clean, modular, reusable. This final review ties everything together: multiple modules, cross-module interfaces, generic functions, and clean organization. You're ready for any codebase.
why: This review synthesizes every L6 concept into a single well-organized application — proving you can design, structure, and implement programs that scale beyond a single file.
analogy: This well-organized application is like a professional kitchen — ingredients (models) are stored in one area, prep work (tasks) happens in another, and plating (display) in a third. Each station has its own tools and expertise. The head chef (main) coordinates everything without getting their hands in every pot. A clean kitchen produces great food; a clean codebase produces great software.
try_it: Add a `priority` system: create a Priority enum (Low, Medium, High) in models. Update Note to include priority. Add `filter_by_priority` in reporting. Add a `summary` module that prints a formatted report of all notes grouped by category. Notice how adding features is easy when modules are well-organized — you touch the relevant module, not a giant blob of code.
tips: Dependencies flow one way: main → high-level modules → low-level modules — never circular
Each module file should be readable in isolation — a newcomer should understand it without reading the entire codebase
Interfaces define contracts BETWEEN modules — they're the glue that holds the architecture together
common_mistakes: Creating circular dependencies — module A uses B, B uses A. Break the cycle by extracting a shared interface
Putting too much in main — main should be thin: create objects, call functions, maybe 5-10 lines total
Making every type and function pub — private by default forces you to think about what's truly API vs implementation
